title: Practice Period 3 - Sandokai
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett invites listeners to explore how their minds categorize and divide experiences into pleasant, unpleasant, and neutral, leading to division and suffering. By studying this process, they suggest we can develop greater flexibility and fluidity in our perception of reality. The goal is not to change or achieve a specific state, but rather to cultivate awareness of the process itself, allowing us to appreciate the "good emptiness" that arises from recognizing the interconnectedness of all things.
topics: two monks carrying a woman across a river

sentences.text: *That is our mystery.
Do not pass your days and nights in vain.*
I'll send you the link to this, actually.
I was just listening to Pema Chodron.
She has a new book out called Welcoming the Unwelcome.
She's referring to traditional teachings, but it's very practical.

She and Oprah are friends.

But that's also good, because we've tried, I think all of us, to do all the practical stuff.
Yet something feels incomplete.
Something feels not quite solvable by practical stuff.

If this gives us some hint or some feeling or some direction towards a deeper dive into the nature of whatever, the nature of self, the nature of reality, maybe that'll be helpful in a way that's somehow beyond the practical.
At least I'm hoping so.
Anyway, I appreciate your slogging through this with me.
I feel bad sometimes bringing this stuff up.
It's archaic, weird stuff that is important because the tradition says it is.
And yet it has a certain power, right?
So here we are.
Yeah, Chris.

And they wander over in the dark and chant the English version in the morning.
At four o'clock they head over and chant in Japanese, which is really, really difficult.
But it's a text that is really drawn on at Tassajara.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah.
No, it's a central text.
It's just not very accessible.
It's just interesting.
Yeah, and that's beautiful, the way they do that there.
The Japanese are enchanted with this odd rhythm that goes slower and faster and slower and faster.
It's hard to do.
So anyway, I've divided the text into clumps of eight lines each, which is more or less when the topic changes.
Tonight I want to talk about the third eight-line chunk, which starts at line 17 on the front handout.
I want to recommend that in general, when you're working with an original text, you divide it up somehow, because they are a little overwhelming, this one big piece of stuff.
So divide it in some way that seems logical to you.
It doesn't really matter if it's the way that some scholar would divide it, or who knows how the author would divide it.
In this case, we don't even know how the author would divide it, beyond that there are lines of five characters.
So this column on the left with all the Chinese, that's how it was originally written.
There's no punctuation, there are no chapter headings, there are no sections, there's no 2.2 or anything like that.
It's just a block of Chinese.
So it's good, I think, to find ways to divide things up.
Before I talk about that, I want to bring our mind back to the last section we looked at last week, from lines nine to 16, which is more or less about the second skandha.
The mental factor of feeling, or feeling tone, is more accurate.
It's the way the mind so automatically and so quickly divides everything up into things that are pleasant and things that are unpleasant.
Technically, there are also things that are neutral, but I think we hardly notice those because we're so busy being worried about pleasant and unpleasant.
And then from there, as we all know so well, this cascade of thoughts and opinions and views and tribalism emerges, and wars emerge, right?
So it's cute that we have such silly preferences in a way, but it's also not too cute, right, because it's a root of such human suffering.
So the text is talking about really studying that, really noticing the way the senses interact with the world, noticing the way we evaluate things like sights and sounds.
We're trying to figure out their quality and their form, and we're trying to figure out if we like them or not, right?
Line 14 talks about things being pleasing or harsh.
And then it ends with this couplet that's a little bit mysterious, which is introducing a theme that we're going to come back to, lines 15 and 16:
*The refined and common speech come together in the dark, and clear and murky phrases are distinguished in the light.*
So dark and light here is another reference to these two underlying topics, philosophical reality topics, of ji and ri.
Dark is this quality of the unknowable interactions of things, the inner penetration of everything, the emptiness of everything.
So it all comes together.
Refined and common are supposed to be talking about things that are opposite, right?
Refined, common, common like coarse.
Somehow the things that seem to be opposites, and from every one of these pairs you generalize out, right, all the opposites somehow come together in the dark.
And yet we're always shining light on things with our consciousness and then we're dividing things up again.

So maybe there is a practical suggestion here, which is that we could get a lot more flexible and fluid about the way we divide things up if we could deeply remember that they're in some fundamental way not really divided in that way.
Really there's some kind of inner penetration, some kind of unity that's below everything.
And so I asked you to do a little homework assignment, which I will leave time to talk about, I promise.
To see if you can notice in an experiential way, what does it feel like when you encounter the pleasant and the unpleasant?
So we'll come back to that.
I just want to give us the setup, because the early Buddhists, in attempting to debunk our preciousness around ourselves, came up with a list of five mental factors.

They say that if you really pay attention in meditation and study this stuff carefully, everything you think is you is actually just a bunch of different experiences that land in these five different categories of experience.
These are the five skandhas that get negated in the Heart Sutra, or emptiness pointed out in the Heart Sutra.
So the second section of the text talked about the second skandha, and now the third section is going to talk a bit about the first skandha.

The five are physical form; this feeling tone business, pleasant, unpleasant; perception, which is touched on here, too; mental formations, the way we assemble everything into all kinds of ideas, which is a long, complex list of different ways that we do that; and mind consciousness, the consciousness that is doing this thinking that we think is me especially.
They say, no, even that is just a faculty of mind that does thinking and notices thoughts, and that's not you either.
So it's interesting that he starts, because usually you do things in order, even Buddhists.
He starts with the second skandha, with this feeling tone, pleasant, unpleasant, and now he's moving on to form.
So let me read you this little section again and we'll try to unpack it a little bit.
*The four elements return to their natures just as a child turns to its mother.
Fire heats, wind moves, water wets, earth is solid, eye and sights, ear and sounds, nose and smells, tongue and taste.
Thus with each and everything, depending on these roots, the leaves spread forth.*
The elements that we're talking about here are in an early Buddhist way, and the Chinese had a similar version, of making sense of matter and making sense of physical reality.
They said everything boils down, in this case, to these four elements: fire, wind, water and earth.
They are different things and their functions are different.
So the first two lines remind us that there are these four different things that have some sort of nature to them, some sort of quality, and they have particular functions.
Fire heats.
Wind doesn't do the heating, water doesn't do the heating, fire does the heating.
Wind does the moving, not the other three.
Water does the wetness, not the other three, and earth does the solidity.
One of the traditional meditations is actually to notice and really study yourself that way, too.
A lot of this central theme of Buddhism, remember those three marks of reality, one of them is don't believe in yourself quite the way you think you do.
That's a source of suffering.
So here's a different way to break the self down.
The five skandhas were one way, here's another way.
Here's a bunch of stuff.
We've got heat, so you can tune into your sense of warmth, you feel that.
We know we've got wind, right, we're breathing.
We know we're whatever percent water.
Who are the Star Wars characters that call us ugly bags mostly full of water?
Ugly bags of mostly water, that's us.
And we've got solidity, right, so bones and tissue, that's the earth element.
So we're just a bunch of stuff, and the universe is just a bunch of stuff, and our senses interact with that stuff, right?
Eyes interact with sights, ears interact with sounds, and so on.

So in a way this is a bunch of different ways to break down our experience that aren't our usual way, aren't our usual me, me, me, you, you, you, what do I need here, what do I want, what am I not getting, and so on.
One of the ways to think about this section that can help us, I think, is to recognize that in any given moment, in a very fundamental way, there's only one of six things happening.
Either we're seeing a sight, we're hearing a sound, we're smelling a smell, we're tasting a taste, we're feeling a sensation, or we're thinking a thought.
And that's it.
Nothing else is actually happening.
Then we create stuff from that, right, the mind is very good at creating all the rest of it.
But really in any moment it's just one of those things happening, and we're busily weaving them together.
Another practical thing to think about, if you think about there being six things that we're noticing, is that maybe we're a little out of balance in the way we emphasize just one of those.
We tune out the senses most of the time.
We're pretty big on sight because we want to make sure that nobody's looking at us funny.
But the other senses we hardly notice at all.
And we're really big at which sense, right, the sixth one, so we're lost in this crowd of thinking.
So that's actually a therapeutic thing.
There is practical stuff in here after all.
I take it back.
What if we just balance this out a little bit?
There's a deeper point here that we're not even a me, but we could balance this out a little by spending more time noticing the senses.
So that's one of my suggestions for this next week.
I made the suggestion the first week to go outside, because it seems to be easier for us outside, and open up all the senses regularly.
What do I see?
What do I smell?
What do I feel?
And then drop the "I" out of it.
What is seen?
What is felt?
What is smelled?
What is tasted?
So it's all just about breaking down our experience in a different way.

In the Suzuki Roshi book, he talks about this, and he talks about a Japanese term which I'd never heard anywhere else, and I couldn't find a reference to it, but I don't read Japanese, so that's probably why.
He says the Japanese Buddhist way to think about this is that any moment of perception is broken down to this atom of momentariness, which he calls Gokumi.
It might be the same idea as a Dharma, Dharma with a little d.
Do you know about the way Dharma has these multiple valences?
It's a confusing word in the tradition.
In English, it's usually distinguished with the capitalization.
Dharma with a big D is the teachings of the Buddha, and Dharma with a little d is a moment of experience.
So maybe that's the same as Gokumi.
But the cool thing about meditation is that it makes it a lot more possible for us to slow down our perceptual process and notice our moments a little more fully.
And then, depending on these roots, the leaves spread forth.
So that makes sense now, right?
We're gathering and perceiving and percepting, and the world's made of these elements, and we're interacting with them with our senses.
So we're setting down some kind of roots, and in Buddhism they talk about wholesome roots and unwholesome roots, so that's implied here.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** We're sending down roots, and those roots are going to lead to something, right?
So this is also karma.
Karma, cause and effect, is in the text, especially in section two.
We send down some kind of wholesome roots, and wholesome leaves spread forth.
With unwholesome roots, we know what happens there: nasty, curled-up, dead, smelly leaves.
And Suzuki Roshi, in the seventh talk, goes a couple of lines further.
He doesn't agree with my eight-line thing, exactly.
He includes the next two lines, so let's look at those, because it's on the same topic.
Then he says, Sekito says:
*Trunk and branches share the essence.
Revered in common, each has its speech.*
Let's see if I can find my notes about that.
I thought about that a little bit.
So, trunk and branches share the essence.
What's the essence?
Tree-ness, I guess.
We could say a tree is just a tree.
I'm just a person.
But we could also say a trunk is different from a branch, right?
We could have a cartoon picture in our mind of a tree with a straight trunk and a horizontal branch, and I can tell you that's the trunk and that's the branch.
So they seem to be different things.
Here's the idea of difference again.
And yet, if you think about it much longer, it gets a little more complicated, a little more suspect.
Can we really tell the difference between a trunk and a branch?
What are the defining characteristics of a trunk and a branch?
You could say, well, the branch is horizontal.
But we've all seen trees where the trunk goes horizontal, and that's not a branch, that's a trunk, right?
And even if we can tell that's a branch and that's a trunk over there, they come together somewhere.
If we get out our microscope and try to figure out where the trunk cells end and the branch cells start, we probably can't tell.
It's all blended together.
So here is another way of saying we have these conventional ways of dividing things up, trunks and branches, and yet they share an essence.
We can't exactly tell what they are.
That's the same with me and you.
Tim and Ken share the essence, but I think I'm separate, and he probably thinks he's separate, I don't know.
I haven't asked him, but he thinks he's part of me.
And yet we seem to be separate.
But are we separate?
Don't go doing that karate stuff on me.
So that's interesting.
And then the next line is trying to apply that back, yet again, to the way we divide up the world.
*Revered in common, each has its speech.*
Revered in common: this is a pretty interesting thing that we do.
We divide things up into special and ordinary, spiritual and common.
We think this building is a spiritual building and everything's just so.
I sometimes talk about this: people walk in the door and they feel the spiritual energy.
"Ah, yes, it's so good."
And smelly trash cans in the alley behind Railroad Street are not spiritual.
That's common.
And yet it's the same thing, really.
It's the same thing as trunk and branches: they share the essence, and they each have their way of expressing.
So this looks and smells different in Red Cedar Dharma Hall than in the alley behind the restaurant with the trash cans.
And yet, is it really different?
And what happens when we get attached to those categories and really believe them to be true?
Here's an example.
A couple of days ago, one of our neighbors, who is probably experiencing homelessness, spread out all of his blankets and stuff in our back parking lot to get them dry.
It was actually kind of pretty.
They were colorful blankets spread out.
I assume it was a he; there's a guy who sits back there sometimes.
He had a few stuffed animals that were really cute, and actually in good shape, like a white seal and some other white animal.
So is that revered or common?
This person taking care of their things, and the deep connection I feel of concern, like, oh gosh, wow.
And the confusion that we feel: what do we do?
Anyway, I admit I just admired it and moved on, but I wasn't parking back there either.
The whole parking lot was filled with all the blankets.
But then a little later Bob Penny drove up and texted me that he was going to clean it up because he needed to park back there.
And then I thought, oh, it's not spiritual at all.
It's common.
It's junk in the way of Bob Penny parking his truck.
And I assumed he was going to throw it all away.
Seemed sensible.
But you know what he did?
I didn't notice at first, but there's also a shopping cart parked in the corner of the parking lot.
Bob Penny very carefully folded everything up and put it in the shopping cart, and rolled the shopping cart down to the sidewalk so it would be easier for the person to find their stuff.
So it seemed to me, did he see it as more revered?
I don't know.
It's interesting.
So what are the ways we divide things up, and are they serving us or not serving us?
And are they true or not true?
In his book, Suzuki Roshi, and actually this is a collection of talks that were edited, he didn't actually write this book, it came out after he was dead.
But in the book made from his talks, when he's looking at revered and common, he talks about the precepts, which is interesting.
It's one of the interesting sections in there.
He says we tend to make this kind of division in a way that messes us up when we're trying to be ethical.
This is actually a barrier, the way we divide things up so rigidly into revered and common.
And he tells a super famous Zen story, which I've always liked.
But then, tragically, when I was reading it and preparing to recount it to you, I realized it's really a pretty sexist story.
So anyway, here's the story, take it as you will, which is also revered and common, right?
The revered Zen story, which suffers from the common problem of sexism and misogyny that's so laced into everything.
And that gives me an extra sort of common feeling of, well, how come I didn't know that before?
It's pretty obvious.
Anyway, the story is that two monks are preparing to wade across the river at the ford.
There's no bridge.
They're in their traveling clothes, with their sandals tied on, these straw sandals with lots of long fabric to hold them on really well, and their traveling pants that they can pull up.
So they have the right gear to wade across the river.
But there's a woman standing there who wants to get across, and she doesn't have the right clothing.
Maybe she has a kimono on or something.
Somehow her clothing isn't right for wading across the river.

And so one of the monks picks her up and carries her across, and the other guy walks along too, and they cross the river and set her down and keep walking on their way, to the next monastery or something.
Eventually it turns out the monk who didn't pick her up has been stewing over this incident and upset by it.
Eventually he just cracks and he complains.
I think he's supposed to be a junior monk too, so it was a little bit bad that he complained.
He said something like, "Why did you carry that woman?
We can't hold women.
It's against our precepts."
And the monk who did carry her said, "Oh, I put her down back there, and you're still carrying her.
That's the violation of the precepts."
That's the story.
But setting the sexism aside, what are the things that we carry?
Can we get better at setting them down?
And is the whole reason he needed to complain some kind of limited view or confusion about revered and common, about what's spiritual and what's not?
How do we proceed in the world, with its diversity and its complexity, while also honoring the unity and power of awakening?
Those are my comments for now about this section.
Questions or thoughts from you?
Elements, fire, eyes, trunks, branches.
What came up for you studying this?
**Participant:** I just have been wondering the last couple of classes, I noticed that, excuse me, he keeps mentioning speech, like a finite form of speech, clear and murky phrases.
A common hate speech, yeah.
Why is there that focus?
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Well, I don't know for sure, but the idea is probably that there's a difference between something's nature and its expression.
Speech means expression.
So I think it's another point to realize there's something behind everything that's expressed, and not to confuse the expression with its inherent nature, its reality.
That's my take on that.
You're right, it's interesting that they use that verb.
They could have used lots of other verbs besides speech, probably.
Does that help?
**Participant:** Yeah.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** And that's true, too.
In political discourse, we confuse the expression with the nature of the person all the time.
**Participant:** So, you talked about the essence of the branches and the trunk.
Is the essence in the acorn as well?
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, the essence is in the acorn, and the sun's in the acorn, and the rain's in the acorn, right?
The essence is everything, and yet the only way we can talk about it is by dividing things up.
Saying that's a tree, that's an acorn, that's a branch.
But yeah, absolutely.
**Participant:** So then there's the essence in the ash after you've ruined the tree.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, Dogen has some stuff to say about firewood and ash, yeah.
**Participant:** Yeah, not to be confused by the idea that one thing leads to another, even though it seems like it does.
So that's another version of this, isn't it?
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah.
On the one hand, one thing leads to another.
There is time, there is temporal stuff.
On the other hand, each moment of time has its own inherency, its own quality, its own essence.

**Participant:** I don't know if this is a characteristic of Western language, that we take everything, or we try to turn everything into nouns, and thereby fix the existence at a certain stage, while I believe other languages treat it a bit differently.
I also experience it differently: I see everything as a process, at least for short periods of time.
Instead of the tree as it is, I see the process from birth to death.
I see buildings as inhaling and exhaling people, and growing up and collapsing.
So if we let go of the fixedness of that specific moment, it's a little bit easier to understand this text.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** That's a wonderful point.
Yeah, we do fix things with our language.
It's really a process, yeah.
**Participant:** And language really fixes the way we think.
It really impresses us from a very early age, and it can impact how we process things mentally.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Right, exactly.
And so language is a quintessential example of this idea, right?
That's how we're making things into separate things.
Yeah, great point.
Exactly, it's all a process.
Trees are growing, we are coming and going.
Let's circle up into groups of three and discuss what you noticed about pleasant and unpleasant experience in your life.
What was that like?
What happened?
Could you drop below the story and feel the feeling of the way you're dividing things up?
Any surprises or interesting things there?
And if you didn't formally write stuff down, that's okay.
You can probably think of some pleasant and unpleasant things that happened without too much trouble.
We could have a couple of fours, that'd be okay.
Mary, why don't you join these guys here?
Hey, Wayne, why don't you join them, and Mary join these guys, because it's a richer conversation with more than two.
That's empty, that's good.
Yeah, very good emptiness.
So what's the most important thing?
Separating everything.
